newsitem.title: UK: Thousands march in N.Ireland amid violence.
newsitem.headline: Thousands march in N.Ireland amid violence.

text.p: Tens of thousands of pro-British Orange Order members marched to the drum and the pipe on their most cherished anniversary on Saturday after a night of attacks blamed on Irish republicans.
The 80,000-strong Protestant order called off marches in four volatile zones of Northern Ireland after Catholics threatened mass demonstrations against what they say is intimidation by the marchers.
The Orange Order's unprecedented decision to foresake what it calls a birthright raised hopes that its "Glorious 12th of July" anniversary would pass off peacefully.
U.S. President Bill Clinton praised the Orange Order for rerouting its parades and condemned "inexcusable" overnight attacks on security forces and two youths.

IRA gunmen wounded five members of the security forces in a gun and bomb attack on Friday night when Protestants lit bonfires on the anniversary eve. Two Protestant teenagers were also shot by unidentified republican attackers.
The head of Northern Ireland's biggest political group, the pro-British Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), condemned the Irish Republican Army (IRA) and its political arm, Sinn Fein.
"It just underlines the evil intent of Sinn Fein/IRA," David Trimble told the BBC.
Britain's Northern Ireland security minister, Adam Ingram, added: "These incidents are clearly designed to heighten tensions at a time when feelings within the community are running high."
Spokesmen for Loyalist groups close to pro-British gunmen said they feared the wounding of the two teenagers would provoke retaliation in an atmosphere already charged with tension.

"Here we have an overtly sectarian attack which, I think, is an attempt to provoke loyalists to the defence of their areas. We will have to wait and see what happens," said Gary McMichael of the Ulster Democratic Party.
Loyalists, who are supposed to be observing a 1994 truce, say they are fighting to defeat the IRA's campaign to end British rule of Northern Ireland, which has a Protestant majority.
They have been blamed by police for a series of botched attacks against Sinn Fein in recent months.
Sinn Fein, which wants British rule scrapped and Northern Ireland united with Ireland, had campaigned for many of Saturday's marches to be cancelled.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair urged Sinn Fein to get the IRA to declare the ceasefire that would admit it to peace talks.
"In the last two days, the Orange Order by their decision have opted for hope. I congratulate them. Sinn Fein can now respond," Blair told a youth conference in Britain.
Sinn Fein has been barred from Northern Ireland peace talks since the IRA ended a 17-month truce in February 1996 to resumed its campaign against British rule of the province.

The Orange Order scrapped one march in Belfast and parades in Newry and Armagh and rerouted another in Londonderry in a move that ended decades of stubborn refusal to accept objections by Catholics who say such demonstrations are triumphalist.
On Saturday the Order also called off a parade in Dunloy, 50 miles (80 km) north of Belfast because of a protest by 200 Catholic nationalists, as well as another march in Bellaghy.
An Orange leader called for unity after the decision to reroute the parades exposed divisions within the order.
Grand Master Robert Saulters said: "At such a time like this we ask for the whole-hearted support and undivided loyalty of our brethren and all those who place confidence in us.
"Remember, United we stand divided we fall'."
But republican gunmen were out on the steets late on Friday night and injured three soldiers and two police in a carefully planned ambush in North Belfast.
The teenagers, one aged 14 and the other 18, were wounded in shootings early on Saturday as they attended a Belfast bonfire, one of hundreds which burned across the province until dawn.
Security forces said a mortar was fired at a British army helicopter pad in the staunchly Irish nationalist county of Armagh on the border with Ireland, but no one was hurt.
Saturday's festivities commemorated a 1690 Protestant victory over Catholic forces at the Battle of the Boyne which ensured that a Protestant ascended the British throne.
